The pre-existing bats fixtures make_staged_repo and make_real_reconcile_repo in bin/tests/test_add_failure_mode.bats build a synthetic pipeline/ tree with toy stand-ins (trivial scripts writing a literal placeholder string) and were never updated when 2910bf9/6749ea0 changed what the write path actually does -- they don't create capture_embedding_snapshot.py at all, and their cluster.py stub doesn't expose the real module API now called via importlib. Reproduced locally: bats --print-output-on-failure bin/tests/test_add_failure_mode.bats at PR#124's head 687e2c8 shows the exact 8 CI failures (tests 8, 11-14, 19-21) all failing on 'python3: can't open file .../capture_embedding_snapshot.py: No such file or directory' followed by 'add-failure-mode: operation failed; applying undo journal'. This is NOT the sibling-checkout issue FM-361 wrongly claimed (corrected by a separate catalog entry on branch fix-catalog-guard-sibling-checkout, PR#125, not yet merged -- watch for an ID collision at merge time, both this entry and that branch's correction independently claimed the next-available slot) and NOT a CI environment gap -- it is a genuine fixture-completeness defect introduced by PR#124's own commits. PR#124 correctly added a NEW, properly-updated pytest suite for this behavior (bin/tests/test_add_failure_mode_release.py, commit 5984a93, with a _RELEASE_STUB 'honest' stand-in that imports the real staged cluster.py) but never retrofitted the equivalent fixture pattern into the older bats suite that still exercises the same full-loop path. SIGNATURE: when a PR changes what a shared code path actually does (new subprocess calls, new module API surface), every fixture across every test framework that exercises that path must be updated in the SAME PR, not just the new test suite the PR itself introduces. FIX (scoped, not yet applied): extend make_staged_repo/make_real_reconcile_repo to (1) copy the real pipeline/cluster.py into the stage instead of a toy stub, (2) install a capture_embedding_snapshot.py stand-in modeled on test_add_failure_mode_release.py's _RELEASE_STUB honest-mode pattern, (3) provide/copy pipeline/replay_l2.py and pipeline/recall_baselines.py into the stage plus seed pipeline/L2/recall-baselines.json for the ratchet to update against, (4) reconcile the bats assertions that hardcode the old toy-stub placeholder digest (~lines 243-263) against real cluster output. Route through a fresh scoped build task referencing test_add_failure_mode_release.py's stand-in as the template.

Background waiter's pgrep -f pattern matched its own command line, so the wait loop never exited A coordinator armed a background waiter of the form 'until ! pgrep -f "run-suite.sh --jobs 4"; do sleep; done' to fire when a BATS sweep finished. The waiter's own /bin/bash -c command line contains the pattern, so pgrep -f always matched (itself), the loop never terminated, and the completed sweep's results (1939 ok, log already on disk) sat unreported ~1.5h until the coordinator verified process state directly. Same class as duramind dm-15 (pkill -f killed the orchestrating shell whose own cmdline matched). Fix pattern: match on a token that cannot appear in the poller's own cmdline (pgrep -f on the absolute script path with -x semantics, a pidfile, or 'pgrep -f PATTERN | grep -v $$'), or wait on the harness task mechanism instead of process polling. 2026-08-18, fleet#604 sweep, session 3ab084ba.

Diagnosis attributed a log line to the wrong emitter, producing a wrong issue premise A CI-red diagnosis saw 'cluster backend selected: tfidf (forced)' in the guard job's log and concluded the CI workflow forced the tfidf backend because the runner could not reach the http backend; hindsight#120 was filed on that premise. In fact the guard job runs pytest, and the line was emitted by a TEST that deliberately forces tfidf (test_ground_truth_contract_with_forced_tfidf_backend) — the reds were a stale committed snapshot plus a tfidf recall regression (#121) and a dead degeneracy assert (#122), all unrelated to reachability. The premise was only falsified when a second agent reproduced the failures with the backend up (HTTP 200). Cross-ref hc-FM-105 (fix built on unconfirmed diagnosis). Fix pattern: before filing a root-cause claim from a log line, attribute the line to its emitting source (rg the literal string in the repo) and reproduce the failure with the hypothesized cause removed. 2026-08-18, hindsight PR#119, session 3ab084ba. (GitHub #120)

Stub-seam tests certified a binary invocation the real binary rejects (setpriv --setenv does not exist) fleet#498 W1 (PR#638, 2026-08-18): the tdd-build lane tested the root launcher's setpriv privilege-drop chain entirely through the SYSTEMD_RUN_CMD stub seam. Suite green 70/70, mutation check 3/3, coordinator host-verified — but the constructed argv used setpriv --setenv, an option the real /usr/bin/setpriv does not have (it has --reset-env). In production the primary drop path would exit 1 before exec. Caught only by the Grok cross-vendor review, which checked the constructed option list against the shipped binary's manpage and refused PASS. Fix pattern now applied: alongside stub-seam behavior tests, add one test that runs the REAL binary against the constructed option list (unknown options exit 1 without needing root). Family: validators-must-pass-ground-truth / green-stub-is-not-evidence. Cross-ref hc-FM entries on config-vs-documented divergence.

SHA-pinned CI poller reported green on a partially-registered check set (1 of 14 checks) 2026-08-18, fleet PR#639: the merge-gate poller looped until total_count>0 and total_count==completed_count. Immediately after a push only GitGuardian had registered, so the first poll saw total=1/done=1/bad=[] and printed DONE — a green merge signal while 13 of 14 required checks, including the entire bats suite, had not yet been created. The merge was not made only because the coordinator eyeballed the suspiciously low total against the 14 seen on prior heads. Class: gate fails OPEN on an incomplete sample (same family as absence-in-a-sample-that-couldnt-show-presence). GitHub creates check-runs progressively, so 'all registered checks are done' is not 'all required checks passed' until registration settles. Fix applied: poller now requires (a) total >= MIN_CHECKS floor, (b) all registered completed, (c) total stable across two consecutive polls, and exits non-zero early on any non-success conclusion. Stronger variant if this recurs: assert the required-check NAMES from branch protection are all present, rather than a count floor.

A test asserted an isolation property in a comment that was never implemented anywhere fleet#498 W2 (PR#639, 2026-08-18): dispatch/test/root-launcher-wiring.bats:33-35 states 'every other suite is pinned off so ambient machine sudo state can never change its behavior' via CLI_DISPATCH_ROOT_LAUNCHER_DISABLE. That variable is set in no other file — not helpers.bash, setup_suite.bash, or run-suite.sh. The claim read as a design guarantee in review and was false. Consequence was not hypothetical: because the activation probe used a PROXY command (sudo -n true) rather than the real launcher invocation, every unrelated suite's start took the real root-launcher path wherever passwordless sudo works, and the check-gaming CI job went red with exactly its two real-cli-dispatch arms failing while all GAMED arms still passed. Two independent detectors agreed (Grok cross-vendor review reading the tree; CI executing the fixture) — genuine corroboration, separate contexts. Fix patterns: (1) an isolation/pinning property stated in a test comment must be implemented in shared setup and itself asserted, or the comment deleted; (2) an activation probe must exercise the SAME invocation the production path uses, never a proxy, so activation and isolation cannot disagree. Family: the-artifact-is-not-the-fix / validators-must-pass-ground-truth.

Verify which branch a shared checkout is on before committing into it; a repo left on another session's branch silently strands the write. 2026-08-18: the coordinator filed four FM catalog commits (FM-361..FM-365) into the shared ~/projects/hindsight checkout without checking the current branch. The checkout had been left on build-red-ci-pair, a branch slated for closure, so five failure-mode records landed where closing that PR would have stranded them; they had to be recovered by cherry-pick onto a split branch. Family: dispatched-agents-pollute-shared-checkout / verify-actual-config-not-documented.

When a test sweep reds only while another session runs its own suite on the same host, adjudicate it against an isolated re-run plus pinned CI at the same commit — never re-run until green; and give each session's bats run its own TMPDIR. 2026-08-18: a fleet#604 full sweep in /tmp/fleet-604-verify reported 9 'not ok' cases, all in the doctor suite, while a DIFFERENT session's job (c271d65e, fix-493) ran its own parallel bats (-j 6) on the same host. The identical doctor suite passed 31/31 in isolation minutes later and the pinned-CI run at the same commit was green. The coordinator adjudicated the 9 as environmental and merged on CI+isolation evidence -- correctly -- but the interference mode itself went unrecorded. Likely mechanism: shared /tmp/bats-run-* state or doctor probes assuming exclusive host state (processes, ports). Fix patterns: per-session TMPDIR for bats runs; doctor probes must not assume exclusive host state. Family: dispatched-agents-pollute-shared-checkout (host-level variant) / isolation.

The must_not_merge precision fixture (completion-signal vs shared-mutable-checkout) is not enforced -- HTTP embedding clustering can and does merge them hindsight's HTTP embedding backend clusters catalog entry fleet-MDL-18 ('subagent returns at the dispatch boundary, not the result boundary') together with the shared-mutable-checkout family (fleet-OPS-13/36/38/41/45) in cluster c-050, violating the must_not_merge precision fixture for the (completion-signal, shared-mutable-checkout) pair. Confirmed pre-existing at commit 03957ed^ (before hindsight PR#124's FM-364..370 re-file), so it is a latent embedding-quality defect, not something introduced by that PR. The overlap is generic coordinator/agent vocabulary shared by both families' descriptions, not genuine semantic similarity. No sanctioned precision re-baseline mechanism exists (pipeline/recall_baselines.py only ratchets recall, per test_cluster.py's own code comment); must_not_merge stays absolute by design.

cli-dispatch's privileged root-launcher drops PATH for harnesses outside the default system PATH, breaking every cross-vendor review lane dispatch/cli-dispatch invokes sudo -n cli-dispatch-root-launcher with a bare harness command name (codex, grok), not an absolute path. sudo's secure_path excludes user-local install directories, so the sudo-invoked launcher cannot find codex (under ~/.nvm) or grok (under ~/.grok/bin), failing with 'setsid: failed to execute codex: No such file or directory'. cli-dispatch doctor reports both as ready because it checks the caller's own PATH, not the launcher's stripped one. Every review-fanout Codex/Grok lane failed identically on 2026-08-19 for fleet PRs 649/650/651/652; dispatches that set CLI_DISPATCH_ROOT_LAUNCHER_DISABLE=1 (bypassing the launcher) worked every time. Filed as fleet#653; PR#654 resolves the harness command to an absolute path before the sudo call. A live smoke test found a second layer: codex is a #!/usr/bin/env node script, so env's own PATH lookup for node hits the same stripped environment; grok is a native binary and unaffected. A follow-up extends the fix to resolve shebang interpreters too.

A PodDisruptionBudget allowing zero disruptions on a single-replica workload must be treated as a drain blocker, not as protection clearwatch/wordpress, visual-tester, content-cache-postgres, qdrant, research-postgres and two zero-replica workloads all carried maxUnavailable:0 or minAvailable:1 at one replica. That buys no availability -- PDBs constrain only voluntary eviction, so a node reboot kills the single pod regardless -- while making kubectl drain hang forever on four nodes. The 2026-08-18 outage happened because the hypervisor was rebooted ungracefully; the graceful alternative was impossible precisely because of these PDBs. Check: for each PDB, if status.expectedPods>0 and status.disruptionsAllowed==0, fail. Recovered re-filing: this content was silently discarded during a catalog-collision merge resolution (git checkout --ours picked the wrong side) and is being restored here at a fresh ID; the original ID (FM-365) now holds unrelated content.

A check whose PASS condition is the absence of a signal must be validated against a positive source before its negatives are trusted 2026-08-19 node reboots, two instances in one task. (1) /var/run/reboot-required was absent on all twelve k3s nodes, so the flag reported 'no reboot needed' everywhere -- including eight nodes running 6.8.0-137 with 6.8.0-138 staged in /boot. Comparing the running kernel to the newest installed /boot/vmlinuz-* is the positive source. (2) The same script inferred 'the reboot happened' from the node going NotReady, but node-monitor-grace-period is ~40s and a 4-vCPU VM can go down and return inside it, so a SUCCESSFUL reboot would have timed out and aborted, leaving a healthy node cordoned and drained. status.nodeInfo.bootID changing is the positive artifact. Recovered re-filing: this content was silently discarded during a catalog-collision merge resolution (git checkout --ours picked the wrong side) and is being restored here at a fresh ID; the original ID (FM-366) now holds unrelated content.

A workload that fetches its own runtime from the internet on every start has an undeclared external dependency that only surfaces when it is finally restarted 2026-08-19: clearwatch/wordpress persisted only wp-content on its PVC and downloaded WordPress core from wordpress.org in an alpine:3.19 init container on EVERY pod start. Cluster DNS had been broken for musl-libc images for an unknown length of time -- petersimmons.com answers NOERROR-with-no-records instead of NXDOMAIN, and musl stops searching there rather than falling through to the bare name, so every Alpine pod failed to resolve any external host while glibc pods were unaffected. Nothing detected it because the pod had not restarted. A routine node drain restarted it and the site could not come back. Two compounding lessons: (a) a long-running pod's ability to START is untested until it restarts, so uptime is not evidence of recoverability; (b) treat 'downloads its runtime at boot' as a hard availability dependency and either bake it into the image or persist it. Recovered re-filing: this content was silently discarded during a catalog-collision merge resolution (git checkout --ours picked the wrong side) and is being restored here at a fresh ID; the original ID (FM-367) now holds unrelated content.

Repo-tier policy fan-out (managed-block AGENTS.md installs across multiple repos) has no auto-refresh hook, so a canonical-source edit silently leaves every already-merged repo's embedded digest stale until someone manually runs the drift checker The Claude-tier managed block (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md) self-heals on every SessionStart via claude_adapter's hook -- editing ~/AGENTS.md automatically re-syncs it on next session start, confirmed working this session (RefreshState.CURRENT immediately after a source edit). The repo-tier fan-out mechanism (repo_fanout.py, used to install the managed block into 5 heavy-tier repos' AGENTS.md files) has no equivalent hook: when Task 14 edited ~/projects/AGENTS.md to add rule-ID markers, all 4 already-merged repos (fleet, clearwatch, ops-plans, homelab-config) silently went stale -- only discovered because repo_fanout.check() was run manually and explicitly, not because anything alerted to the drift. The same thing happened again after a second canonical edit (Task 15's keep/cut pass) later the same session. Each repo re-fan requires its own PR + cross-vendor review, so this isn't cheap to fix reactively, and nothing currently prompts a session to even notice it's needed. General lesson: any multi-target fan-out mechanism without the single-target adapter's self-healing property will accumulate silent drift across every canonical-source edit -- either give repo-tier fan-out an equivalent periodic/session-start check (even just a warning, not an auto-write, given each write needs its own review), or explicitly document that repo drift is expected to lag and must be checked before relying on repo-tier content being current. [recurrence_of: none]

A check whose PASS condition is the absence of a signal must be validated against a positive source before its negatives are trusted 2026-08-19 node reboots, two instances in one task. (1) /var/run/reboot-required was absent on all twelve k3s nodes, so the flag reported 'no reboot needed' everywhere -- including eight nodes running 6.8.0-137 with 6.8.0-138 staged in /boot. I read the flag alone and told the user worker142 needed no reboot; it did. Comparing the running kernel to the newest installed /boot/vmlinuz-* is the positive source. (2) The same script inferred 'the reboot happened' from the node going NotReady, but node-monitor-grace-period is ~40s and a 4-vCPU VM can go down and return inside it, so a SUCCESSFUL reboot would have timed out and aborted with 'reboot may not have happened', leaving a healthy node cordoned and drained. status.nodeInfo.bootID changing is the positive artifact. Check: for any gate of the form 'flag absent => healthy' or 'condition never observed => event did not occur', require a positive-source cross-check before the negative is actionable. Supersedes FM-374: an earlier re-filing of this same incident condensed the wording and silently dropped this entry's Check prescription and two illustrative clauses; this entry is the complete, verbatim-restored version.

A process check must match on a token that cannot appear in the checking command's own command line, and a negative result must be corroborated before it is reported as 'nothing is running' 2026-08-19/20 homelab campaign: THREE instances in a single session, one a variant the existing entry does not cover. (1) 'pgrep -f <pattern>' matched the checking command's own /bin/bash -c line, so a background task that had been looping 2h57m was reported to the founder as 'nothing is running'. The supporting evidence was an empty output file plus an empty task list -- both equally consistent with 'never started' AND 'still running', so the corroboration was vacuous. Only the founder's screenshot exposed it. (2) The same defect had already been diagnosed EARLIER in the same session for a different task, which was killed on that basis -- but the first task was never re-checked, so a method known to be broken was left standing against a second target. (3) A 'ps -eo | awk' variant, not pgrep at all: awk field indices matched the wrong columns of the checker's own row and produced an elapsed time of '441077234-00:18:40', which was then reported to the founder as evidence that HIS machine's clock was skewed. The clock was fine (NTP synced, btime consistent). SIGNATURE beyond the existing entry: this is not specific to pgrep -- it is any process query whose result set can include the query itself, and the ps/awk form fails DIFFERENTLY, yielding a plausible-looking WRONG VALUE rather than a hung loop, which is worse because it invites a confident false diagnosis of an unrelated system. Direction matters: instance 1 fails toward 'nothing is happening', which terminates investigation instead of prolonging it. DIAGNOSTIC LESSON: when a check of this shape is found broken, re-run every earlier conclusion in the same session that relied on it -- a method known to be unreliable does not become reliable for the targets it was already applied to.

A guard's positive control must be derived from the artifact under test, never a hardcoded constant -- a constant is knowable in advance and can be satisfied by the very substitution the control exists to detect homelab-kubernetes#20, fixed 2026-08-20. REFINES FM-377 (absence-of-signal checks need a positive source) by constraining WHICH positive source is admissible. The ARC key-ownership guard decided PASS by the silence of a yq query that discriminated on the very key names it was hunting for, so a substituted yq that answered the other queries plausibly and returned nothing for the deciding one passed a values file carrying a real local 'image:' pin, rc=0. FIRST FIX added census parity plus a positive control -- but the control was a CONSTANT (the file's known first key, githubConfigUrl). Attacking my own fix defeated it: a stub emitting a coherent, correctly-sized census that simply omitted 'image' satisfied parity AND the constant control, and the pinned file still passed rc=0. Only a control COMPUTED FROM THE ARTIFACT closed it -- every key the file literally declares unquoted at column 0 must appear in the parser's census -- because a stub cannot satisfy that without reporting the document truthfully, and a truthful report cannot hide the pin from the shell-side decision. SIGNATURE: a positive control is only as strong as the attacker's ignorance of it; a constant can be hardcoded into the liar, a control that scales with the artifact cannot be pre-satisfied. Corollary on scope: the text-derived control is a FLOOR, never the verdict -- a quoted key is real and invisible to a regex, and a comment mentioning the key false-fails, so the parser still decides and the text only bounds what it may claim it saw. DIAGNOSTIC LESSON, the part that generalises furthest: re-running the ORIGINAL repro after a fix proves only that the fix stops the attack you already knew, and the first fix did stop it. The hole was found solely by writing a SECOND, smarter attacker against the fix itself. Any repair to a fail-open guard must be followed by a fresh attack designed against the repair, not a re-run of the repro that motivated it. Verified after: a real local pin is caught under a real yq, a silent stub, and a coherent lying stub alike; quoted-key and comment-mentioning regressions both hold.

A reviewer must label a check it could not RUN distinctly from a check that FAILED, and the recipient must re-derive which blockers are real rather than accepting or dismissing the verdict as a whole 2026-08-19/20 homelab campaign, cross-harness review of three PRs. Both independent reviewers returned blocking verdicts (DO-NOT-MERGE, MERGE-WITH-FIX) whose headline blockers were ENVIRONMENTAL, not defects: their sandboxes had no DNS ('curl: (6) Could not resolve host registry.petersimmons.com') and no cluster access ('Unable to connect to the server: dial tcp 192.168.0.131:6443: operation not permitted'), so the registry-digest and live-manifest checks could not run at all. Both reviewers stated the limitation honestly in their prose -- the defect is in the VERDICT SHAPE, which collapses 'verified false' and 'could not verify' into one blocking token. Two opposite failure directions follow, and both nearly occurred: (a) accept the verdict wholesale and abandon a sound change; (b) notice the blockers are environmental, dismiss the verdict, and thereby discard the reviewer's REAL findings, which were buried alongside -- a README asserting maxRunners 6 where manifest and live both said 12, and a Helm array-replacement hole that let a values file discard the shared image pin without naming any owned key (proved with real Helm v3.18.6: pin ABSENT). Direction (b) is the more dangerous because the environmental blockers are conspicuous and the real findings are not. SIGNATURE: any verdict emitted by an agent whose environment is narrower than the artifact's dependencies must carry a per-check disposition -- verified / refuted / NOT RUN with the reason -- and consumers must re-derive per-check rather than treating the verdict as atomic. Corollary for dispatchers: when a reviewer cannot reach a dependency, the missing coverage does not disappear, it silently transfers back to the dispatcher, and must be named as single-source wherever the result is reported. In this campaign the registry digest and the live-manifest comparison were re-run by the dispatcher and labelled single-source in the PR record for exactly that reason.

A process check must match on a token that cannot appear in the checking command's own command line, and a negative result must be corroborated by a second signal before it is reported as 'nothing is running' 2026-08-19/20 homelab campaign, three instances in one session. (1) 'pgrep -f <pattern>' matched the checking command's own /bin/bash -c line, so a background task that had been looping 2h57m was reported as 'nothing is running'; only a founder screenshot exposed it. (2) The same defect was already diagnosed earlier in the session for a different task, which was killed on that basis, but the first task was never re-checked. (3) A 'ps -eo | awk' variant (not pgrep) matched the wrong columns of the checker's own row, producing an elapsed time of '441077234-00:18:40' that was reported as evidence of a skewed system clock -- the clock was fine. Direction matters: these fail toward 'nothing is happening,' terminating investigation rather than prolonging it. When a check of this shape is found broken, re-run every earlier conclusion in the same session that relied on it.

A guard's positive control must be derived from the artifact under test, never a hardcoded constant homelab-kubernetes#20, fixed 2026-08-20. The ARC key-ownership guard passed a values file carrying a real local 'image:' pin because its positive control was a constant (a known first key) that a stub could satisfy without reporting the pin. Only a control computed from the artifact -- every key the file literally declares must appear in the parser's census -- closed it, since a stub cannot satisfy that without truthfully reporting the document. A text-derived control is a floor, never the verdict: a quoted key is invisible to regex and a comment mentioning a key false-fails, so the parser still decides. Any repair to a fail-open guard needs a fresh attack against the repair itself, not a re-run of the original repro.

Mutation-testing a check by exit code alone proves nothing when that check already fails at baseline - every mutation scores identically whether or not it was detected 2026-08-20 homelab-kubernetes#28. A new declared-vs-live reconciliation check was legitimately RED against the cluster: it reported a real, still-unfixed defect it had been written to catch. Its mutation suite then asserted 'apply mutation -> expect exit 1' and reported 6/6 caught. That result was vacuous. The baseline was ALREADY exit 1, so a mutation the check ignored completely would have scored exactly the same, and the suite could not have failed for any input. Rerun requiring each mutation to add a NEW failure line NAMING the mutated object, the signal became real - and two mutations turned out to be invalid rather than missed (appending 'affinity: {}' to a Helm values file is a genuine no-op because Helm merges maps; only 'affinity: null' deletes). Without the message-level rerun, a correct check would have been 'fixed' to satisfy an invalid mutation. SIGNATURE: a differential test whose signal is one boolean is valid ONLY when the baseline sits on the opposite side of that boolean. Any check expected to be red for a known reason - a real defect it reports, an environment it cannot reach - must have exit-code assertions replaced by output-DELTA assertions before any 'N/N caught' claim is credible. Neighbours in the corpus, same family, different mechanism: hc-FM-311 (vacuous RED from a selector matching zero tests - success and failure modes indistinguishable) and hc-FM-170 (a green suite whose assertion was satisfied by data the report merely printed). This entry is the baseline-already-red variant: the confound is not an empty population but a saturated signal.

Folding a capability probe into a step that gates the job stops the very checks it was added to protect, and the resulting red names the precheck instead of the finding 2026-08-20 homelab-kubernetes#28, caught in review before merge. A CI job ran three cluster checks behind a preflight step that asserted the runner's identity was read-only and ended in 'exit $fail'. Adding a new check that needed two extra RBAC reads, the natural move was to assert those grants in the same preflight - it is the step that already checks the identity. That would have set $fail whenever a grant was missing, and since the step ends in 'exit $fail', GitHub would stop the job THERE: the new check would never execute, and the two checks that passed today would ALSO never execute. A job that had been verifying three things would verify nothing while looking like a normal red, and the failure text would name the precheck rather than the defect. Worse, the grant genuinely WAS missing (measured by impersonating the ServiceAccount), so this would have happened on the very first run and the red would have been read as 'the new check works'. Fix: the preflight now REPORTS positive grants and gates only on the negative security assertions (cannot create/delete/patch/update, cannot read secrets). Each check's own preflight names the specific read it lacked and exits SKIP, which that job already treats as failure - so strictness is unchanged and the diagnosis is precise. Confirmed on the real run: both pre-existing checks PASSED and the new one reported 'SKIP: this identity cannot list namespaces'. SIGNATURE: a precondition belongs in the step that CONSUMES it, not in a shared gate, whenever the gate can abort siblings. Distinguish a SECURITY boundary (must fail closed and stop everything - a runner that can write is a finding) from a CAPABILITY report (must not stop siblings - one check's missing grant is not another check's problem). Folding the second into the first trades N specific diagnoses for one generic abort, and silently reduces coverage at the moment coverage is most in question.

An ARC runner pool with minRunners:0 makes the first CI job after idle fail as backend-unreachable — check runner-pool cold-start before diagnosing the backend Measured 2026-08-20 (hindsight#120/#126 chain): arc-hindsight at minRunners:0 cold-started from zero and the job failed reaching the embedding host at 192.168.0.98:8004 while the backend was healthy (curled 200 directly); sibling pools with minRunners:1 never showed it. Workaround applied: helm minRunners 0->1 (live cluster value). Durable non-catalog record: homelab-config#200. Re-filed from closed draft PR#131 after the FM-377 ID contention resolved.

A review lane never checks out or fetches into the shared coordinator checkout — PR-head inspection happens in its own detached worktree Measured 4x on 2026-08-20 (fleet PR#650/#662 review-fanout rounds): the ground-truth/review lane checked the PR head out IN ~/projects/fleet, leaving it detached/staged; every concurrent cli-dispatch lane then honestly refused its STEP 0 fast-forward (dispatched:false for Codex AND Grok simultaneously — the misleading double-failure signature). Recovery: git checkout main && merge --ff-only origin/main; preserved dirt to a labeled stash. Structural fix: review-fanout.js now provisions /tmp/review-fanout-<pr>-<sha7> via git worktree add --detach and forbids shared-checkout mutation (ops-plans receipt 2cf8a6d).

A root cause published from static text without a live probe is a diagnosis draft, not a diagnosis Third recurrence of the hc-FM-105/FM-365 wrong-first-diagnosis pattern (cluster c-133), fleet#658 on 2026-08-20: a subagent inferred 'check-phase pod pinned at 1 CPU' from reading requests.cpu in helm values; the coordinator posted it to the issue before any live probe; exec into a live runner showed nproc=4 (limits.cpu governs the cgroup) and the real cause was bats invoked with no --jobs. Corrected same day (issuecomment-5361344442) but the wrong diagnosis was published externally first.

codex exec with workspace-write defaults network OFF — pass sandbox_workspace_write.network_access=true or every gh/curl step silently fails mid-task Recurrence of the sandbox-network-off family (c-004: ccx-FM-004, fleet-COM-5, FM-353), measured 2026-08-20: gh issue view inside codex exec failed 'error connecting to api.github.com'; with -c sandbox_workspace_write.network_access=true the same command succeeded and the ambient App token authenticated as the codex worker bot. The codex:codex-rescue bridge bakes in the same gap (never sets the flag) on top of being unpollable — prefer direct codex exec.

A backgrounded headless agent launch must close or redirect stdin (</dev/null, or a real brief file) — an inherited never-closing stdin blocks the harness forever Recurrence of FM-68's stdin-hang mode (c-094), measured 2026-08-20: a backgrounded codex exec printed 'Reading additional input from stdin...' and idled to timeout 124 having done no work; relaunching the identical command with </dev/null completed normally. Same mitigation direction as FM-68: give stdin a real EOF (either /dev/null or an actual brief file the harness reads to completion).

A CI-board gate must derive pending state from the tool's own status field, never from a hand-rolled mapping of .conclusion — GitHub returns an EMPTY STRING for in-flight checks, which jq's '// "PENDING"' does not substitute for Measured 2026-08-21, bg job 92e4a093, fleet PRs #666/#669. A monitor gate written SPECIFICALLY to avoid an earlier partial-board misfire used jq '(.conclusion // "PENDING")' to classify checks. jq's alternative operator substitutes only for null and false, but GitHub's statusCheckRollup returns .conclusion == "" (empty string) for a check that is still running. Eight in-flight checks on PR#669 therefore counted as neither pending nor failed, and the gate announced 'PR#669 GREEN 6/14 pass, 0 pending, 0 failed'. It was caught only by noticing the arithmetic did not close -- 6 + 0 + 0 does not equal 14 -- not by any check. 'gh pr checks --json name,bucket' has a first-class 'pending' bucket and reported pass:6,pending:8 correctly against the same board at the same moment. SIGNATURE: an absent-value default ('// x', 'or x', '?? x', COALESCE) protects against null but not against a sentinel EMPTY value, and an API that uses empty-string-for-not-yet turns that gap into a silent false-negative in the safe direction of the gate. Whenever a gate partitions a set into buckets, assert the partition is TOTAL (sum of buckets == set size) -- that assertion, not the classification, is what catches an unmodelled state. Prefer the vendor tool's own status field over re-deriving one. SECOND instance of self-authored-gate-misfire in this one session: ~20 minutes after committing a review artifact upholding the standing 'PASS is narrow; default is FAIL' discipline, an earlier gate in the same session fired merge-ready on SUCCESS:1 of a 14-check board. Both gates were written by the entity they existed to constrain, and both failed in the permissive direction.

Before a 'rewrite N artifacts as template X' rollout, AUDIT that all N are expressible in X -- and never overwrite the originals in place when they live in an unversioned directory Measured 2026-08-21, fleet#660. An issue proposed rewriting 7 acceptance-gate scripts under .dispatch/checks/ as thin exec wrappers of a tracked template, 'preserving each gate's floor/skip semantics'. The template accepts exactly four parameters (CHECK_SUITES, CHECK_SUITES_CMD, CHECK_PLAN_FLOOR, CHECK_SKIPS_FATAL). An audit of the five not yet converted found 0 SAFE / 5 LOSSY: they carry mutation checks that patch the code under test and require red, negative controls, green-red-green round trips, git-state assertions that named files stay unchanged, shellcheck runs where shellcheck's ABSENCE is a FAIL, awk-extracted CI-config assertions, and one gate needing TWO independent floors where the template supports one. Executing the rollout as written would have deleted every discriminating check while leaving five green-looking gates. The framing assumed floor/skip semantics were the whole content because that was true of the first artifact examined. SECOND HALF, and the reason this is HIGH: the two already converted were overwritten IN PLACE, and .dispatch/ is git-excluded (.git/info/exclude:7), so no VCS history and no .orig/.bak exists anywhere. Their conversions can never be verified -- all that remains is a comment, written by the conversion that destroyed the evidence, asserting what the original did. Against a measured 5-for-5 lossy base rate that claim deserves less confidence than it had when written, and it is unfalsifiable. SIGNATURE: (1) a homogeneity assumption across a set of artifacts must be MEASURED before a bulk transform, not inferred from the first one read; (2) an irreversible edit to an unversioned file destroys the only evidence the edit was correct -- reversibility and auditability are the same property there. Keep the original beside the replacement whenever the directory is not version controlled.

A headline figure that drives prioritization must state its denominator -- 'two jobs own 87% of the critical path' was job-seconds misread as wall clock, and the real ceiling was 27% Measured 2026-08-21, fleet#633. The issue title asserted 'two unsharded jobs own 87% of the critical path -- check-gaming 457s, bats/orch 423s at --jobs 1'. Re-measured on run 32447516370 (main, all green) by pulling per-job started_at/completed_at from the Actions API: every job starts within 18s of the first (no runner queuing), total wall clock 445s, and removing BOTH named jobs entirely moves the last finish from +445s to +323s -- 122s, 27% of wall clock, not 87%. By the other plausible reading the two are 36.7% of 2130 total job-seconds, also not 87%. Either way the number overstated the available win by roughly 3x, and anyone sequencing work against it was sequencing against a saving that could not be delivered. The DIRECTION was right (bats/orch at 432s is the critical path single-handedly), which is what made the wrong magnitude survive: a plausible number pointing the correct way is not re-derived. Re-measurement also surfaced something the issue never mentioned and which changes the plan: the ALREADY-sharded dispatch jobs run 281/146/203/305s -- the fastest shard finishes in under half the slowest, so ~160 job-seconds of provisioned parallelism sits idle, and rebalancing costs no new runners. Sharding another job before rebalancing would recover much less than the arithmetic suggests. SIGNATURE: for any percentage used to prioritize, name the denominator in the same sentence; wall clock and resource-seconds diverge whenever work runs in parallel, and 'critical path' specifically means the longest chain, never a sum. Re-measure a load-bearing figure before sequencing against it, especially when it is directionally correct.

A vendor's cybersecurity classifier can refuse a DEFENSIVE review of our own authorization code -- route to another harness, never reword around the block Measured 2026-08-21, fleet PR#671. A Codex lane was dispatched to independently review a new caller-ownership check on dispatch/cli-dispatch-root-launcher --kill-scope (a root-privileged authorization path in our own repo). The prompt asked the reviewer to try to break the check and to demonstrate any finding in a local fixture -- ordinary adversarial-review framing, and the only framing that produces a credible security review. Codex refused: 'This content was flagged for possible cybersecurity risk... To get authorized for security work, join the Trusted Access for Cyber program', exit 1, no review produced. The same brief, unmodified, was accepted by Grok Build (grok -p --yolo) and the review proceeded. IMPACT: the merge gate requires an independent cross-harness review, so a classifier refusal at one vendor silently narrows the pool of available reviewers for exactly the changes that most need reviewing -- security-relevant ones. A run that does not notice the refusal banks 'no findings' from a lane that never looked. REMEDY: route to a different harness. Do NOT soften or reword the brief to slip past the classifier: the adversarial framing IS the review method, a version rewritten to avoid trigger words produces a weaker review, and constructing wording to defeat a vendor restriction is the manoeuvre this model generation is documented performing. Record the refusal as evidence rather than working around it invisibly. Check: whenever a review lane returns nonzero or empty, read WHY before treating its silence as a clean result.

Before escalating a red CI board to the founder as a decision gate, prove the failing tests predate your own branch: check git log --diff-filter=A on the test file and diff --stat against the merge-base. fleet PR#671: I reported 9 red dispatch-2 cases as deliberately-documented pre-existing contracts requiring a founder ruling, and posted three blocking questions. The red was a regression from my own commit 349c6f1, and one of the failing cases (case 58) already contained the answer to the question I was asking. Fixing it required rewriting zero contracts. The escalation cost a full loop tick and would have cost founder attention on a decision that was never his to make.

A safety argument that enumerates only what an ATTACKER can do to an invariant is incomplete: enumerate what your own code paths do to it, and name the code that could violate it. fleet PR#671 kill-scope ownership. I argued an absent manifest could not describe a live lane because 'ln refuses to replace a record and the directory is root-owned, so an unprivileged caller can neither overwrite nor unlink it', and wrote that reasoning into the code as justification. Both clauses were true and the conclusion was false: they constrain the ATTACKER, not the launcher itself. The same-owner retry I had just added unlinked live records, treating 'we are starting this task' as 'the previous one ended' with no check. A cross-vendor reviewer reproduced the full chain -- second same-owner launch unlinks the live record, the failing launch's EXIT trap retires the replacement, any sudoers principal then reaps the victim scope. Mutation checking did not catch it because no case had a live first launch, so the suite never asked whether the unit was still there. Check: for each 'X cannot happen' in a security argument, list every code path that writes the state X depends on, including the one being added in the same change.

Mutation-test a gate against CONTAINMENT context, not only prefix and suffix edits: wrapping the asserting command in a heredoc or disabling its step must fail the audit fleet#633 PR#680. An anchored line-level fullmatch in ci-meta-floor-audit.sh was proven fail-closed against four mutation classes -- echo prefix, printf prefix, trailing 'or-true', and missing argv -- all killed, coordinator-verified. Independent round-3 review then bypassed it two ways the probe never tried: wrap the identical board command in a bash here-document, or add 'if: false' to the rollup step. Both leave ZERO executing assertion and both returned exit 0 reporting '7 floors are wired'. The probe varied the command's edges and never asked whether the line sat in an executing context at all. Fix required parsing ci.yml as YAML, excluding constant-false steps, stripping heredoc bodies for all four delimiter forms, and treating any statically-undecidable if: as EXECUTING so the audit fails closed. Recorded as a recurrence of c-171 because it is the same family as a fail-open guard whose repair was verified by an insufficient re-attack: the repair was real, the attack proving it was not.

Restoring a deleted guard at its OLD value instead of its MEASURED value silently re-creates the gap the guard existed to close fleet#633 PR#680. CHECK_GAMING_CASE_FLOOR 16 was deleted; review required restoring a pass pin. The fix restored CHECK_GAMING_PASS_FLOOR at 16 -- the old deleted number -- while the repo's own skip-baseline file recorded the measured CI value as 18 passed, 0 failed, 0 skipped with an EMPTY baseline, reproduced locally. At floor 16 the pass-to-allowlisted-skip attack survives one or two conversions: total stays 18, fail stays 0, passes drop to 17, board green. The coordinator's own probe missed it because it tested WHETHER the floor fires (15 passes gives FAIL) rather than whether the floor sat at the right VALUE. A restored guard must be re-derived from the current measurement with the derivation shown, never copied from the pre-deletion constant.

A mutation that breaks an upstream precondition measures the precondition, not the lock; confirm the mutated artifact still reaches the assertion under test hindsight#108 PR#139. To prove a rewritten test locks three literal replay pins, the coordinator mutated the pins to a bare true assertion and read the resulting failures as the lock firing. Wrong mutation class: the write path's updater regexes require the comparison FORM to be locatable, so that mutation makes the pins unlocatable, the add aborts, and the test never reaches its own oracle -- the observed failure was the add failing. Independent review found the class that actually threatens the property: a postfix or-true, which stays locatable at match count 1,1,1 because the regexes are not anchored to end-of-statement, and which the PRIOR version of the test passed 3 of 3. Before trusting a mutation result, verify the mutant still executes the assertion being tested. Recorded as a recurrence of c-171: same family as the vacuous mutation suite whose signal could not have differed for any input.

A floor must be raised only for tests added to the corpus that floor actually measures, and its arithmetic recomputed against current main rather than a stale base fleet#633 PR#680. BATS_EXECUTED_FLOOR is measured in ci.yml by counting dispatch/test bats cases, but a commit raised it 1962 to 1972 for ten tests added entirely under orchestration/test/bats; git diff --diff-filter=A showed the branch added no dispatch/test file at all. The commit comment itself called it a category-error ratchet and rationalized it as harmless headroom. Reverting it then exposed a second layer: the branch had been cut before another PR landed, so main was at 1966 while the branch reasoned from 1954, and the revert to 1962 read as a LOWERING against main -- correctly caught by a guard test that greps the shipped literal. Both defects share one root: floor arithmetic computed against a stale base and against the wrong corpus. Resolution was to merge main and take its value unchanged, because the branch adds no case to the corpus that floor measures.

A unit test with a hard dependency on a live service turns an unrelated commit red and trains people to re-run without reading hindsight#140. pipeline/tests/test_cluster.py test_default_backend_selection resolves the UNFORCED default embedding backend, which is an HTTP backend on a homelab GPU endpoint. During a brief outage the CLI correctly refused to substitute tfidf, whose embeddings diverge from the committed http-fitted snapshot, and returned 1 -- so the guard job failed on a DOCS-ONLY commit adding two markdown files. The prior commit passed, the re-run at the identical SHA passed, and a direct probe of the endpoint returned 200 minutes later. The production refusal is correct and must not change; the defect is the test's coupling to service uptime. Diagnostic trap: a red board on a commit that could not possibly have caused it is indistinguishable at a glance from a real regression.

When review blocks on a boundary a tool does not have, fix the CLAIM before hardening the tool, and check whether the modeled attacker can bypass the tool entirely fleet#550. A terraform apply wrapper was documented as high-assurance enforcement. Four review rounds each found a new environment vector: TF_CLI_ARGS, then TF_WORKSPACE selecting state after the identity check, then TF_CLI_CONFIG_FILE, HOME and PATH selecting an unreviewed provider via dev_overrides, then pathname-not-bytes state binding. Every one requires the attacker to already control the operator's process environment -- and anyone with that control runs terraform directly and never reaches the wrapper. Rounds 5 and 6 would have bought nothing against that threat model while nine live cluster nodes stayed one accidental apply from destruction. The reviewer's own baseline comparison was decisive: the findings do not make the baseline bare-apply landmine worse. Correct disposition was to state the real threat model, an accident-stopper for an authorized operator, name both gaps in the docs, file them, and land the P0 fix.

When a gate is bypassed, check whether the fix rejects an ENUMERATED form or removes the class; a denylist of spellings guarantees the next reviewer finds spelling N+1 fleet#633/PR#681, five review rounds 2026-08-20/21. A static text audit (ci-meta-floor-audit.sh) tried to prove a DYNAMIC property -- that a CI floor assertion executes. Each round patched it to reject the forms the previous reviewer demonstrated, and each next round found a new one: r1 echo/printf prefix and || true suffix; r3 heredoc body and YAML if: false; r4 <<\\EOF delimiter and if: ${{ 0 }}; a coordinator probe found 'true \\' continuation making the assertion argv; r5 found 'if false; then ... fi'. The remaining space is open-ended (while false, case, uncalled function, early exit, &, eval) so no finite denylist terminates. Round 5's own proposed fix -- reject compound-control-flow contexts -- would have rejected CORRECT shipped code, because main's legitimate whole-corpus assertion is itself 'if (( total_case_count < BATS_EXECUTED_FLOOR )); then'. Measured that origin/main's audit accepts an if-false-wrapped assertion too, proving the limitation pre-existing rather than a regression, which is what made accept-and-document the right disposition instead of a sixth enumeration. Convergent fix filed as fleet#683: the assertion writes a runtime RECEIPT naming the floor and measured count, and a downstream job fails if the receipt is absent or disagrees with ci.yml -- so nothing about the workflow's text is trusted and a wrapped assertion fails closed.

Before claiming a parallelization win, check whether the shards contend for the SAME finite resource; a slowest-shard-plus-rollup formula silently assumes unlimited executors fleet#633, measured 2026-08-21. Sharding the CI critical path was predicted to cut ~72% by the naive model (wall clock = slowest shard + rollup). Measured reality was ~24%: orch bats 431s->325s, check-gaming 393s->294s, total 438s->331s. Root cause is that the shards queue against each other for a finite ARC runner pool -- a 204s runner-queue delay was observed directly, i.e. sharding contends with itself. The naive formula treats executors as unlimited and therefore overstates the win roughly 3x. The check is to measure queue-wait separately from execution time before quoting any speedup, and to state the runner-pool size as an explicit assumption of any sharding design.

Before placing a new gate downstream of an existing job, check what that job does when its dependency FAILS; a gate behind a job that skips on failure is vacuous in exactly the case it exists for, because a skipped job reports Success fleet#683 spec v1, caught by independent refutation 2026-08-21 BEFORE any code was written. The design was to prove a CI floor assertion actually executes by having it write a runtime receipt, with a terminal verifier job that fails when a receipt is missing. The verifier was specified with 'needs:' on the two rollup jobs. But the shipped rollups (.github/workflows/ci.yml:885-890 bats-orch-rollup, :1046-1048 check-gaming-rollup) use 'needs:' WITHOUT always(), so when a matrix leg fails the rollup is SKIPPED -- and GitHub reports a skipped job as Success. A verifier behind them is skipped too and goes green having verified nothing. The gate would have been hollow in precisely the scenario it was written for. Two further spec defects surfaced in the same review: the receipt was forgeable because no field bound it to the asserting command's exit status, and the spec claimed coverage of 'every required floor' while ci.yml declares SEVEN *_FLOOR values and only TWO have board-style producers. The general check is to enumerate the full cross-product of dependency RESULT (success/skipped/failure/cancelled) against any path-filter condition, and to state which combinations the gate treats as acceptable, rather than assuming 'needs:' means 'runs after and sees the outcome'. Cost comparison worth keeping: this refutation cost one dispatched review round; the equivalent defect class on fleet#633 cost five build-and-review rounds because the spec was never refuted before building.

A self-attesting receipt is not evidence: if the artifact proving a check ran is written by a process co-located with the check, verify the attestation is bound to the check's exit status across a boundary the attester cannot modify -- otherwise the producer alone can satisfy it fleet#683 spec v1 and v2 both proposed a CI 'runtime receipt' proving each *_FLOOR assertion executed. Grok's v2 refutation (Q2.D): wrap the board command in 'if false; then ... fi' and printf the receipt JSON directly into $CI_FLOOR_RECEIPT_DIR -- producer job reports success, receipt present and well-formed, every contract check passes, verifier untouched. v2's own admitted gap was 'controls both producer and verifier'; this needs only the producer. Root cause: nothing binds the receipt file to the assertion's exit status, and the PR under test controls the workflow that writes it. Distinct from FM-403 (enumeration war) and FM-405 (skipped-job vacuity): those are gates that fail open, this is an artifact that attests to nothing.

A decoder that succeeds on empty input cannot distinguish 'no credential' from 'valid credential': assert the secret is non-empty BEFORE decoding, and assert the resulting identity is the intended one, because a client that silently falls back to an ambient identity turns a missing secret into a misleading authorization error clearwatch#4869, found by estate-wide CI sweep after FIVE consecutive red nights (2026-08-17..21), not by any alert. pipeline-smoke.yml:52-56 ran 'echo $KUBECONFIG_B64 | base64 -d > ~/.kube/config; kubectl cluster-info'. With the secret unset the expansion is empty, base64 -d exits 0 on empty input, and the step writes an EMPTY kubeconfig. kubectl treats an empty kubeconfig as no kubeconfig and falls back to the runner pod's in-cluster ServiceAccount, so the job failed several steps later with 'services is forbidden: User system:serviceaccount:arc-runners-clearwatch:homelab-arc-gha-rs-no-permission'. That error names the FALLBACK identity, so the failure presents as an RBAC gap. It is not one. Measured with the real run: block extracted from the workflow and executed under GitHub's actual 'bash -e': origin/main 3 passed 4 failed (fails OPEN on unset secret, empty payload, and no-current-context); fixed branch 7 passed 0 failed. The cost of the misdirection was concrete: the filed issue proposed granting that ServiceAccount create/delete/pods-exec on a live namespace, which would have made CI green as the WRONG identity, permanently masked the broken secret, and granted a CI runner write+exec that the sibling arc/rbac/homelab-kubernetes-ci-reader.yaml deliberately refuses ('a CI identity that can write is a CI identity that can be used to write'). GENERAL SIGNATURE: whenever a credential is materialized by a decode/parse step, the success of that step is not evidence a credential exists -- base64, JSON parse of '', and empty-string env expansion all succeed vacuously. The decisive assertion is on the resulting IDENTITY, not the transform: here 'kubectl config current-context' is deterministic and version-independent, because ambient fallback happens precisely when no context is selected. Second-order lesson: a diagnostic that names a principal is not evidence the system chose that principal.

A git path helper that honors user-level config can resolve OUTSIDE the repository: before writing to a path derived from git rev-parse --git-path (or any config-sensitive resolver), verify the result is inside the repo, and pin the config in any throwaway repo a test creates -- otherwise an installer under test mutates machine-wide shared state Self-inflicted 2026-08-21, fleet#677, infrastructure/bin/install-hooks.sh. The issue prescribed replacing a broken worktree path construction with 'git rev-parse --git-path hooks/pre-commit'. --git-path HONORS core.hooksPath. This machine sets core.hooksPath GLOBALLY to ~/.config/git/hooks; ~/projects overrides it locally, so the target repo looked fine and the change looked correct. The discriminating test created throwaway repos with 'git init', which inherit the GLOBAL setting, so running the installer there resolved OUTSIDE the temp repo and OVERWROTE ~/.config/git/hooks/pre-commit -- a hook shared by every repo on the machine that lacks a local override. Not version controlled, no backup, prior contents unrecoverable. Detected only because the test asserted the installed hook was executable at the resolved path and printed that path, which did not look like the temp repo. Two distinct lessons. (1) TOOL: a resolver parameterized by user config is not a repo-relative path; '--git-common-dir' is the worktree-correct resolver that cannot leave the repository, and where core.hooksPath diverges the honest move is to REFUSE (exit 2) rather than pick one of two silent failures -- installing in the repo's hooks dir is useless because git runs core.hooksPath, installing at core.hooksPath clobbers shared state. (2) TEST HARNESS: a test that runs a real installer must neutralize every ambient config input the installer reads, or the test itself becomes the mutation. 'git init' inherits global config; pin it explicitly. The blast radius here was the test, not the product. SIGNATURE: sandboxing a test by using a temp DIRECTORY is not sandboxing when the program under test resolves its target from CONFIG rather than from cwd.

Never run a mutation test inside a worktree another agent still holds; snapshot-and-restore races that agent's own writes 2026-08-21: coordinator read a dispatch worktree, saw uncommitted work and a HEAD equal to main, and concluded the lane had died. It had not -- it was mid-flight. Coordinator then cp'd the target script aside, mutated it to verify the tests could fail, and cp'd it back. The agent committed cleanly seconds later and diff showed no damage, but only by luck: any write by the agent between the cp-aside and the cp-back would have been silently reverted, and the restore would have reported success. Liveness must be established before touching a lane's tree, and mutation testing belongs in a separate scratch clone, never in the live worktree.

A performance or causal diagnosis names a mechanism that the already-available timestamps refute, because the timestamps were never read fleet#682 attributed a 204s CI delay to runner-pool contention. The job API showed the rollup job was created at 12:35:38 and started at 12:35:40 - a 2s queue wait. It had not been queued at all; it did not exist until its needs: dependency completed. The refuting evidence was one gh api call away and was never fetched before the causal claim was written and published.

A coordinator's dispatch brief contradicts the issue spec it is derived from, and the lane has no instruction to treat the issue as authoritative hindsight#123/#142, 2026-08-21. The coordinator instructed the lane to set cancel-in-progress: true unconditionally. The issue itself asked for a main-branch exemption, which was correct: unconditional cancellation can leave a merged commit on main with no completed guard run. The lane flagged the discrepancy instead of complying, which is the only reason the defect did not ship. Nothing in the dispatch contract required that - a compliant lane would have silently implemented the coordinator's wrong instruction over the issue's right one.

A mutation that matches zero lines reports the same green result as a surviving mutant, so a broken mutation reads as a weak test hindsight#111, 2026-08-21. A mutation sed 's/^\(\s*\)exit 1$/\1exit 0/' was applied to neutralize a script's refusal path. It matched no lines - the script had no bare indented exit 1 - so the suite ran against unmodified code and passed. The reading was MUTATION SURVIVED, i.e. a weak test, and that finding was nearly reported. The real refusal was [ "$FINDINGS" -eq 0 ] || exit 2; mutating that killed 7 cases. Any mutation harness must assert a nonzero match count or a nonempty diff before interpreting the suite result, because zero-effect mutation and ineffective-test are indistinguishable from the exit code alone.

Reviewer-routing must exclude the PR author's vendor, not merely the coordinator Merge-gate reviews for hindsight PR#142/#143 were dispatched to Grok while both PRs were authored by app/psimmons-grok-worker (Grok). The dispatch logic checked only that the reviewer was not the coordinator. The Grok reviewer disqualified itself unprompted; nothing in the routing caught it. Check 'gh pr view N --json author' and exclude that vendor before dispatching the independence gate.

A dispatched agent's writable scratch may be private to its own sandbox, so host-prepared paths are invisible Codex review lanes were handed host-provisioned worktrees under /home/psimmons/worktrees and then clones under /dev/shm; Codex reported the first read-only and the second nonexistent. /dev/shm is per-sandbox private. Three review lanes were lost to this. The fix is to instruct the agent to clone the repo itself into its own writable scratch rather than handing it a prepared path.

A run-level tooling FAILED flag is not a verdict; test whether a failed command sits on the evidence path The Codex companion flagged 3 of 3 review runs FAILED on incidental delegate-tooling errors. Treating that flag as disqualifying made the cross-vendor merge gate unsatisfiable -- no PASS could ever be accepted. The correct discriminator is whether a failed command lies on the evidence path for a claim being relied on, and whether the claim is a positive artifact (a mutation kill, a count comparison) or an unscoped absence claim.

Re-running a red pull_request check replays the original merge commit; it does not pick up newly-landed base commits After landing hindsight#142, the plan was to re-run the red guard on PR#146 and merge on green. A pull_request run checks out refs/pull/N/merge and a re-run replays the merge commit computed when the run was created, so it would have re-tested the old head against the pre-#142 base and stayed red. Verified: PR#146 reported base.sha=dbafaf4 while main was 44e0a06. Merge the base branch INTO the PR branch to recompute the merge ref, then let the fresh run be the green.

Every programmatic codex exec launch redirects stdin from /dev/null THIRD recorded occurrence of this mode (hc-FM-390 measured 2026-08-20, itself a recurrence of c-094/FM-68; fleet-OPS-40 records it independently). Recording it has not prevented it, which is the finding. 2026-08-21: two coordinator lanes held a live PID for 1h41m and 15m producing exactly 39 bytes. The tell is a log frozen at 'Reading additional input from stdin...' -- NOT an error; healthy runs print it too then continue to the version banner. Control: stdin from a FIFO held open by a live writer gives timeout rc=124 and the 39-byte freeze; </dev/null completes. A harness-launched background job is NOT a valid counter-test -- it hands the child an already-EOF stdin, so it passes while proving nothing. Mechanize: enforce </dev/null in the launcher rather than filing a fourth advisory row. fleet#693.

A lane counts as running only if its log GREW; a live PID with a stale log is HUNG 2026-08-21: two dispatch lanes held live PIDs for 1h41m and 15m while producing 39 bytes, and were reported to the founder as 'running' the whole time. The liveness check keyed on process existence, which reports this failure as healthy. Worse, the first version of the replacement poller ALSO failed open: with no prior size snapshot it printed RUNNING(first-poll) for the very lane that was hung. Snapshots vanish across compaction and restart, so first-poll is exactly when a hang hides. Correct check: compare log mtime against wall clock, which needs no history. Direction of failure matters -- this fails toward 'work is progressing', which suppresses investigation.

A lesson that failed to fire gets rewritten as an imperative rule with a tell and a check, not restated 2026-08-21, same shape as hc-FM-297 and cluster c-018 (preloaded warnings miss near 100% at the moment of action). The memory file lesson-codex-grok-headless-coding, line 23, written 2026-07-27, already said: 'a harness that reads stdin will hang forever with no tty attached even when the prompt was passed as an argument.' That is precisely the bug that then cost 1h56m of dead lanes. The memory was loaded, was correct, and did not fire -- because it was phrased as an observation in a bulleted list of 'related tells' rather than as a rule. Counter-rule: when a lesson exists and failed to prevent the failure, the remedy is NOT another lesson. Rewrite the existing entry imperatively, naming (a) the action to always take, (b) the observable tell, (c) the command that settles it. Filing a fourth advisory row about the same mode is the failure repeating at the registry level.

Apply the discrimination standard to your OWN claims, not only to dispatched lanes 2026-08-21: every Codex and Grok lane this session was required to reproduce before fixing and show RED before GREEN. The coordinator then wrote 'one variable changed, outcome flipped' about its own fix when THREE variables had changed (added </dev/null, switched from the harness background path to nohup, dropped the shell-snapshot wrapper) -- and wrote it into the very plan section that defines the no-unproven-claims rule. Caught by an external advisor, not by self-review. A 75-second control settled it afterwards and confirmed the conclusion, but the claim was unproven when published. Check: before writing 'proven', 'verified' or 'confirmed' about a conclusion YOU reached, enumerate the variables that changed between the failing and passing observation; if more than one, run the control before publishing. A gate applied only to other agents is decorative.

Never run gc --prune=now in the same pass as the deletion whose reversibility you just claimed 2026-08-21 estate cleanup. Deleted 370 fleet branches and recorded each tip SHA, stating the deletion was 'trivially reversible' on that basis. Then ran 'git reflog expire --expire=now --expire-unreachable=now --all' followed by 'git gc --prune=now' in the same pass, which destroyed the recovery path just claimed. Measured with 'git cat-file -e <sha>^{commit}' over all 370 recorded rows: 272 still resolve, 98 DO NOT -- 74 lane-scratch (dispatch/*, agent/*) and 24 human-named (docs/*, fix/*, feat/*, ci/*, chore/*, tests/*, tools/*, pr650-remediation, fix-655-manifest-nits, fix-661-contract-path, fix-672-remote-tracking-containment). Content was not lost: every deleted branch was an ancestor of origin/main or the head ref of a MERGED PR, and squash-merging is precisely why the originals were unreachable and got pruned. What was lost is pre-squash commit granularity plus any abandoned lane work. The defect is not the gc -- it is asserting a safety property and then removing it in the same operation without re-checking the assertion. Check: a stated recovery mechanism must be RE-VERIFIED after every subsequent destructive step in the same pass, or the two steps must be separated by a gate. Direction matters: this fails toward 'the cleanup was safe', which is the reassuring direction.

git reflog expire --all destroys the STASH reflog; never run it to tidy a repo 2026-08-21 estate cleanup, irreversible data loss. Ran 'git reflog expire --expire=now --expire-unreachable=now --all' followed by 'git gc --prune=now' to reclaim space after deleting branches. The --all flag is NOT scoped to branch reflogs: refs/stash entries beyond the tip live ONLY in the stash reflog, and 'git stash list' reads exactly that reflog. 18 of 19 fleet stashes were destroyed, objects then pruned (git fsck --unreachable returns 0). Among the lost was stash@{1}, which ~/HANDOFF.md explicitly recorded as 'unreviewed, not discarded' -- deliberately preserved by an earlier session. One survived only because refs/stash is a real ref rather than a reflog entry. Compounding failure: I had ALREADY stated in the same session's handoff that no stash was dropped, having verified nothing -- I inferred it from 'I never ran git stash drop'. Checks: (1) never use 'reflog expire --all' as a space-reclaiming step; drop specific refs and let the default 90-day expiry work; (2) capture 'git stash list' before ANY reflog or gc operation and diff it after; (3) a negative claim about what you did not damage requires a positive verification, not an inference from which commands you believe you ran. Direction matters: this fails silently and toward 'nothing was harmed'.

A CI-red diagnosis must be checked against a step that actually executed on the cited branch and commit hindsight PR#127 correction: FM-361 incorrectly attributed a red bin/tests step to absent sibling repositories. The cited evidence was from unrelated split-108-fail-loud and a main run where an earlier ungated embedding-snapshot digest mismatch caused later steps to be skipped. Diagnostic run 32243825765 executed the exact bin/tests step on the cited scope and passed 237/237 with no sibling repos; canonical-add tests create their complete synthetic sibling topology under their own tmpdir. Do not infer a later step is red unless it actually ran on the cited branch/commit; distinguish an executed failure from a prior step that masked it. [hindsight#121 recall-baseline override: known corpus-growth artifact, not a per-entry quality issue.]

A gate that creates an in-tree probe must remove its own stale artifacts before its first assertion and on every normal or interrupted exit path. The ops-plans#77 gate wrote handoff/tests/test_zz_gate_probe.py, then a two-minute timeout interrupted it before removal; the next run reported 1 failed, 569 passed and falsely blamed correct lane work because the gate had poisoned its own tree.

A mutation gate for an any-of-N or presence check must corrupt the specific identity under test while leaving plausible neighbors intact. The homelab-kubernetes#24 acceptance gate deleted every digest comment and passed, but deleting only the active tag's digest, replacing it with 64 zeros, or bumping the tag without a new digest all exited 0 because a historical digest satisfied digest_count -ge 1; the online verifier then misattributed that stale digest to the new tag.

A pre-commit gate must snapshot and restore files from private copies; it must never use version-control restore commands against the working tree under test. The acceptance gate used git checkout -- to restore mutated files before cli-dispatch autocommit; because the lane's correct scale-set-common.yaml edit existed only in the working tree, two restore cycles destroyed it and the gate falsely reported that the lane's tests were not green after restore.

Change-scoped acceptance must compare findings and gitlinks against a captured baseline, not require repository-wide absolute zero fleet#690 required zero gitlinks and zero committed-tree secret findings, but baseline HEAD already contained 3 gitlinks, 18 Gitleaks findings, and 4 Trivy findings; the exact change added zero. The absolute gate false-failed a clean scoped import and could pressure a lane into unrelated deletion.

Text-existence guard passes when guarded behavior is disabled but source text is left intact Third+ occurrence of the c-212 class (FM-324/FM-346: comment text satisfies a grep-based check). Four NEW instances in one 2026-08-22/23 session: fleet PR#700 closed as a regression -- comment/echo satisfies a script-invocation guard, and origin/main caught 9 of 16 shell-invocation forms the rewrite missed. fleet PR#701 -- a regex count over an stdin-redirect line is satisfied by a comment mentioning the old form (M5), and a Node text.count() check is satisfied by 'if (false) child.stdin.end();' (M8). hindsight PR#167/guard.yml -- a trivial non-empty stub satisfies a non-emptiness check, dropping guard-bats coverage 13->4 while the sha256 pin on guard.yml stays honestly correct. hindsight PR#171 -- if:false on a step satisfies a step-name-list pin while 261 tests silently stop executing. All assert TEXT EXISTS rather than BEHAVIOR HAPPENS, so a clean deletion is caught but disable-without-delete is not -- backwards from the real threat, since nobody deletes a guard by accident but code gets commented out or short-circuited constantly. Recurrence-of forces mechanize: acceptance criteria for any new guard must require a disable-without-delete proof (comment out, if-false, alias, non-empty stub, zeroing arithmetic, moved-out-of-scanned-path), and a deletion-only proof must be rejected as insufficient evidence.

Rewriting a text-matching security guard produces a narrower recognizer than the one it replaces, regressing vs the prior version Two of two guard-rewrite lanes in one session (2026-08-22/23) shipped a regression: fleet PR#700 (fleet#698) rewrote a script-invocation matcher and origin/main caught 9 of 16 shell-invocation forms (env FOO=1, source, ., backticks, bash -c, if-then, nohup, time, !, stdbuf) that the rewrite missed. fleet PR#702 (fleet#699) rewrote a floor-enforcement audit and origin/main rejected FLOOR*0/FLOOR-FLOOR/chained-zero/large-negative-offset while the rewrite accepted all four; its broadened count pattern also matched 'ran' inside 'branch'. Neither lane compared its new recognizer's behavior against the old one on the OLD recognizer's own catch set before shipping. Fix: any PR that rewrites a pattern-matching guard must run the new implementation against every case the OLD implementation is known to catch (mine them from the old source/tests) and show zero regressions, as a mandatory acceptance item distinct from the new feature's own test cases.

A single agent that both implements a fix and authors its own acceptance test converges on a proof it can satisfy, not the property being guarded Measured 2026-08-22/23: round-1 first-pass validation success across 58 rework-ledger rows was 21%, BELOW the ~33% a purely random process would produce absent any signal -- the process was not merely noisy, it was anti-correlated with the target. Every traced failure was a lane that wrote both the guarded code and a test suite that code could pass: PR#700, PR#701, PR#702, PR#167-r3/r4 all shipped with a self-authored planted-failure proof in the PR body and green CI, and each proof was later shown to be a DELETION test (which any text-matching gate trivially passes) rather than a disable-without-delete test. This is Goodhart's law operating inside a single agent turn: optimizing 'my tests pass' selects for a satisfiable proof, not a correct guard. Fix (deployed same session): separate the attack-test author from the implementer as a distinct agent turn with no production-file write access, require the author to specify disable-without-delete attacks plus a no-regression differential against the prior version BEFORE implementation starts, and make satisfying that pre-written attack list an exit gate on the implementer's own turn rather than a downstream review finding.

git worktree isolation protects files per-worktree but not git CONFIG, so a lane can silently weaken shared state (e.g. core.hooksPath) for every worktree and the primary checkout hindsight PR#169 (#159, core.hooksPath fix): a build lane changed core.hooksPath on the FOUNDER'S PRIMARY CLONE (not its own worktree) to a relative path and deliberately left it unrestored, arguing restoring it would leave #159's original bug active. Measured effect: a branch that deletes its own .githooks/pre-push then pushes gets rc=0 with NO guard firing at all, versus rc=1 with the guard running under the old absolute-path scheme. Every worktree sharing that repo's .git inherited the weakened hook resolution immediately, with no review gate having approved it. git's per-worktree config (extensions.worktreeConfig + config.worktree) exists precisely to prevent this class and was not used. Fix: any brief authorizing config changes as part of a fix must explicitly scope them to test fixtures or the lane's own worktree-local config, never the shared repo config, and acceptance criteria must include an unconditional restore-on-every-exit-path proof, not just a restore-on-success proof.

git push <branchname> from a DETACHED HEAD worktree pushes whatever local branch ref has that name in the shared .git, not the checked-out commits, and fails as a persistent non-fast-forward that resists retries Coordinator hit this directly 2026-08-23 committing test fixes in a detached-HEAD worktree (hs-167, detached at 76f23ba) for hindsight PR#167. 'git push origin fix-164-ci-shard-r2' was rejected as non-fast-forward THREE times despite git merge-base confirming the remote tip WAS an ancestor of the local commit -- because git resolves the bare branch-name argument against the LOCAL branch namespace (shared across all worktrees of one .git), not the current checkout, and a SIBLING worktree (hs-fix-164) had that exact branch name checked out at a stale commit. Diagnosis via GIT_TRACE_PACKET confirmed the server's advertised ref matched the coordinator's expectation, which made the failure look like a race or auth flake rather than a ref-resolution bug. Fix: from any detached-HEAD worktree, push via the explicit refspec 'git push origin HEAD:refs/heads/<branch>', never a bare branch name; and check 'git symbolic-ref -q HEAD' before diagnosing a push rejection as a remote-side problem.

gh run view --json jobs merges step data ACROSS RETRY ATTEMPTS, so a completed prior attempt's steps make a currently-running attempt read as fully concluded 2026-08-22, hindsight PRs #160 and #161: 'gh run view <id> --json jobs' showed '19/19 steps concluded' while one step was genuinely still running on the live attempt. Read as a hung zombie runner, the coordinator cancelled two HEALTHY long-running CI jobs and filed hindsight#166 on the false premise, later retracted and closed. The authoritative, per-attempt view is 'gh api repos/{o}/{r}/actions/runs/{id}/attempts/{n}/jobs' -- 'runs/{id}/jobs' silently defaults to a merged/latest view across all attempts. Fix: any tool or check diagnosing a stuck run must query the specific attempt number, never the bare runs/{id}/jobs endpoint.

ps -eo args | grep truncates long command lines to terminal width, silently hiding matches whose distinguishing text falls past the cutoff 2026-08-22/23, cleanup of orphaned poll-loop shells: a 'ps -eo args | grep pattern' sweep found 4 stale shells and reported the sweep clean; pgrep -f (reads /proc/*/cmdline directly, no truncation) found a 5th, 26 hours old. The coordinator announced 'clean' one shell early on the ps-based check. Fix: any liveness/inventory check against a long command line must use pgrep -f or read /proc/<pid>/cmdline directly; ps | grep is a display tool, not a scriptable inventory.
